To overcome these limitations, this research proposes novel techniques that facilitate NAS within a more extensive search space. This is achieved by adopting a more condensed search space that incorporates abstract program properties, where similar architectures tend to exhibit similar performance. As a result, NAS can be conducted more efficiently. To facilitate this process, the study also develops a novel and efficient synthesis method for generating neural architectures based on the desired program properties. This research is built around the $\alpha$NAS system, a NAS method integrated within an evolutionary framework, where program properties guide the mutation process. $\alpha$NAS demonstrates promising results by taking a ResNet-34 model and surpassing it through 21 minutes of computation with only a 1gb parameter increase while outperforming models from the same class over yeast classification dataset with a 2.49% improvement in accuracy. Additionally, $\alpha$NAS has the capacity to adapt its program properties to particular datasets, resulting in even better results as shown in experiments.

millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receivers. The proposed method leads to significant performance improvements. Notably, with two receive antennas, we see an average reduction of $ 16.8\% $ in the transmit power needed per message and a rise of $ 60\% $ in the information successfully received. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the designed precoder system functions nearly as well as a fully-digital version even in the presence of difficult transmission conditions.

To address these issues, we've developed a utility function learning method that utilizes expert knowledge through preference learning, learned offline from partially defined values from expert input. driving and drone operation could benefit from distributed machine learning (DML) over dynamically changing networks. Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable model inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this paper, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions to improve DML efficiency in networks subject to change. Our model utilizes a nonlinear weighted power mean aggregation approach rather than the linear aggregation typically employed by previous studies. By using mirror descent based on Bregman divergence for optimization and non-linear aggregation, we maintain the ability to reach an optimal solution. Our work thoroughly examines the WPM's properties and formally proves the convergence of our proposed aggregation mechanism. Our experiments further demonstrate that when the exponent p is greater than one, the WPM-based aggregation significantly enhances model convergence speed and scalability compared to traditional arithmetic mean aggregation under dynamically changing network conditions, without compromising final model accuracy.

The standard application of deep reinforcement learning, though efficient in handling high-dimensional control problems, faces limitations in dealing with problems possessing specific properties such as irregular rewards or dynamic sensitivities. To address this limitation, our approach divides the problem into two distinct phases - planning and imitation - to effectively tackle these control issues. The planning stage involves determining an achievable motion plan with predicted dynamics through targeted sampling within the state space. Subsequently, the imitation stage develops an action policy capable of successfully executing the motion plan while accounting for uncertainty in the state and dynamics. The integration of these stages enables the successful resolution of control problems in complex simulations. Moreover, the imitation stage's capability to generate action policies capable of operating within the system's native sampling distribution significantly contributes to improved performance. We validate the effectiveness of our approach in overcoming control issues in multiple complex simulations.

undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broader audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6500-fold increase in preprints within this time frame, albeit only accounting for a modest 4% of published research. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier exposure to an audience by an average of 14 months and significantly higher citation rates at five times that of non-preprint articles. To alleviate concerns over preprint quality, data shows that approximately 41% of preprints are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals with publication outlets being of equivalent influence to papers lacking preprints. The critical role of preprints in communicating emerging research during recent public health crises is also underscored. The quantitative findings presented aim to provide conclusive evidence of the positive impact of preprints on individual researchers and the scientific community, thus enhancing the efficiency of scholarly communication through accelerated and broadened dissemination of research findings facilitated by internet technologies. These metrics can inform policymakers and researchers in strategically employing and responsibly embracing preprints within their respective domains.

interference, and there has been a lack of a quantitative explanation for how interference impacts capacity and how multiple access methods affect each other. This lack of understanding has led to adopting a simplistic, non-interfering assumption in many recent advancements in wireless communication technology, even when it is clearly impractical. To address this limitation, we developed a general mathematical framework for analyzing the impact of interference in wireless networks. This framework utilizes techniques from stochastic geometry to quantify interference and determine the optimal transmission parameters that maximize throughput in a diversity combining system with variable transmit power, block-fading channels, and a single antenna per transmitter and receiver. In addition to providing a general methodology, we used this framework to investigate previously unreported aspects of interference and adaptive transmission in wireless networks. Specifically, we studied the effects of changes in network parameters on interference and system throughput and derived thresholds for the signal-to-noise ratio ratio that distinguish between high-throughput and energy-efficient modes. Our results demonstrate the significant improvement in throughput and the savings in energy achieved by adapting to interference rather than simply incrementing the transmit power in an interference-blind manner. These findings validate the feasibility of more sophisticated multiple access methods that exploit the dynamic changes in interference rather than simply focusing on minimizing the average interference.

semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Firstly, they expand the label set primarily using uncertain, non-neighboring nodes, which often lacks the potential for positive influence. Secondly, they rely heavily on the last iteration's predictions when generating pseudo-labels for continuation training, instead of leveraging the evolving knowledge throughout the iteration process. To address these limitations, we propose Pseudo-Label Propagation (PLP) - an innovative, two-stage pseudo-labeling framework for graph classification that addresses the aforementioned challenges. Firstly, a selective re-activation strategy is employed to engage high-confidence, local nodes in pseudo-labeling, which utilizes an iterative, shrinking strategy to extract emerging, potentially informative nodes from the constantly evolving model's decision boundary. Secondly, a recursive, look-back strategy is applied to retain the iteration-wise knowledge and integrate it into the predictions of the current iteration, ultimately generating high-quality, contrasting pseudo-labels through a collaborative, transductive training mechanism. Experimental results on six diverse graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed PLP approach surpasses state-of-the-art pseudo-labeling methods, yielding substantial, 5.17% generalization performance gain without and 9.22% generalization performance gain with

For certain values of epsilon, like 0.01 and 0.1, the results reveal that the methods perform comparably, while, for epsilon = 0.001, the results confirm the superiority of Leveraged Quadrature over the Chebyshev method. A novel concept has been developed where the spatial arrangement of layered materials enables the creation of intralayer excitons that cannot spread between layers, thus requiring a minimum of two layers to form. Research into multilayer systems made from materials like t TaSe3 and TaS3 is particularly intriguing as they undergo a structural transformation into a state characterized by large clusters of layered materials, dubbed superstructural clustering. Our study also shows that this clustering of layers in Ta6Ge8 leads to an unusual state, an excitonic insulator, that can be recognized by distinct color changes. Our findings indicate that this material's ability to form large clusters of layered structure allows it to support the formation of intralayer excitons, thus facilitating the emergence of an excitonic insulating state. Moreover, this excitonic insulating state can be reversed when the material is changed back to a non-clustered state by applying a certain amount of pressure, thus making this system useful for the study of excitonic insulating states and other properties in layered materials.

DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are concatenated to produce the complete genome, achieving up to 80% efficiency across 128 nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and speed, paving the way for the efficient assembly of large genomes.

Our study proposes an improved logistic equation with a clearer biological foundation based on cell population dynamics, incorporating discrete and distributed delay terms. The model's global dynamics are fully analyzed and proven to result in all feasible nontrivial solutions converging to the stable positive equilibrium. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is quantified as the conditional intensity of the process, obtained via estimation from a suitable transformed kernel of the process event counts. Notably, this new approach allows even non-Poisson processes to be quantified. The proposed method has several key advantages: it offers a universal way to analyze and assess the validity of subsampling methods for inferential purposes, it enables the comparison of event occurrence between different time periods by peering into the past or near future occurrences of events, and it offers a way to measure the significance of significant events within a detected component or thresholded background. Moreover, this new approach allows even non-Poisron processes to be quantified effectively. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods when applied to both real-life data on air traffic control and simulated data on card transactions.

Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to nondifferentiability. Building on the adaptive sieving strategy from the Exclusive Lasso problem, we introduce a novel HDR Lasso solution that takes full advantage of the problem's sparse nature, solving smaller subproblems in each iteration through the proximal point algorithm, which leverages the problem's nonsmooth terms effectively. Our extensive numerical experiments validate the proposed Adaptive-Sieving Proximal Point Algorithm's robustness across various noise types, as well as its high efficiency, particularly for large-dimensional features, when compared to alternative methods.

Researchers have been puzzled by this phenomenon, as it is typically opposed by the second law of thermodynamics. To address this issue, a new theory called granular hydrodynamics was developed, which incorporates nonlinear dissipation. Although an accurate model for hydrodynamic behavior has been established, determining the boundary between dissipative and non-dissipative behavior, particularly for viscous and hyper-elastic fluids, remained unclear. In a recent study, the research team derived a nonlinear dissipation threshold for two distinct types of fluids, namely viscous and hyper-elastic, by combining the Euler equations with an entropy production principle and nonlinear stability analysis. Interestingly, the obtained results reveal a stark contrast between the two fluids, as only hyper-elastic fluid exhibits a non-dissipative ground state and, consequently, an abrupt increase in wave speeds at high stresses. Nonetheless, the theory predicts that both fluids exhibit similar nonlinear dissipative effects, which might be beneficial for the development of more accurate numerical methods in the future.

Through numerical simulations, this research demonstrates the success of this pricing framework in shifting consumption away from peak hours and optimizing storage system training.

Specifically, we investigate how personalisation impacts researchers' ability to discover new knowledge, make informed research decisions, and maintain research productivity. Given that properties of the emission are heavily influenced by the opacities of the expelled material, recent calls for enhancement in the limited available r-process atomic data have led to an increased need for precise atomic structure information. Two sets of galaxy property measurements were generated. Our results do not support the unification theory and could imply the existence of distinct galaxy populations associated with different AGN classes, particularly those related to large-scale structures.

In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. A human evaluation of TCube's narratives revealed a notable improvement in both narrative coherence and engagingness compared to existing methods. Additionally, TCube's narratives were found to be as accurate as the narration methods developed for specific domains, demonstrating its versatility and success.

workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, and quantum circuits, also exploring the relationships between geometric framework concepts and the variables used to describe these architectures. Furthermore, we define and differentiate between two types of geometric framework concepts: those that enhance computational efficiency through novel implementations, referred to as 'accelerators,' and those that facilitate in-depth system analysis, referred to as 'inspectors.' By applying inspector concepts to analyze a simplified version of the AlexNet architecture, we demonstrate the potential for novel, mechanistic insights into neural networks, such as the correlation between feature map channel numbers and concept complexity.

MA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's kinetic energy ratio to its gravitational energy. This alteration led to increased binary mass and enabled a more precise determination of how a system's mass is generated. Furthermore, researchers created a diagram to represent how a system's mass is correlated with its parent core's kinetic energy ratio. This study also recorded and presented various properties of proto-stellar fragments, including formation mass, thermal to gravitational energy ratio, and velocity dispersion.

To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its spread. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for popularity, we treated the propagation process as a stochastic dynamics model, where search queries interacted with categories through transition probabilities. By calculating transition probabilities from search logs, we simulated the propagation dynamics and compared the simulated curves with actual cumulative distribution functions. As a result, our model accurately captured the natural progression of a rumor's dissemination in two out of three tested scenarios. While our approach bypasses the need for explicit variables, modeling a vast amount of variables can be computationally intensive. To alleviate this issue, we developed a successive modeling strategy, where we refined the model one variable at a time, eliminating errors and improving the fit each time. By applying this cumulative approach, our model converged after just five iterations, resulting in a precise fit with minimal parameters.

The triatomic structure is stable as evidenced by the extremely low frequency of oscillation at around 6 keV. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described.

AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead investigate using symbolic representations derived from feature embeddings. This study introduces a novel method using a trained symbolic surrogate model to generate high-level, interpretable representations of image features, which can then be utilized to explain the predictions of black-box AI systems in visual domains. The method has been successfully tested on two challenging image classification datasets and significantly outperformed several alternative approaches in facilitating feature importance assessment and odd-even analysis through enhanced clustering capabilities.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste by reusing graphene wafers. However, little is known about how epitaxial growth affects graphene's atomic structure. In this study, a range of remote epitaxy experiments were performed under varying conditions to understand how graphene's atomic structure is altered. Utilizing atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, the experiments found that graphene's atomic structure transforms into a moiré pattern and subsequently into a new graphene monolayer with a different atomic configuration. This process occurs through the step-patterned moiré structure's evolution into a unique nanoscale graphene domain pattern. By replicating these experiments using simulations, the findings were validated and explained at the atomic level. This research sheds light on graphene's atomic structure transformation and paves the way for the development of novel remote epitaxy techniques.

influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from both auction types to boost revenue, yet we demonstrate that the benefits of uncredibility are limited. To increase profits, auction participants must accurately perceive the auction's lack of credibility. If there's any doubt, the negative consequences of uncredibility outweigh any potential benefits. Furthermore, when auction participants are unsure about the auction's true nature, the revenue generated is similar to that of a credible second-price auction. If participants correctly identify an uncredible second-price auction as such, the revenue is slightly higher. We show that the difficulty in determining auction format contributes to the prevalence of uncredibility in real-world auctions.

In graphene, which possesses a unique layer structure, quantum interference is remarkably pronounced due to its close resemblance to an ideal two-dimensional electron gas. Recent advancements have made it possible to control local properties through advanced surface engineering techniques. Nevertheless, accurately predicting experimental outcomes requires a detailed microscale analysis, taking into account the impact of surface potential variations. This work employs the finite element method to develop a tool for analyzing the local properties of surface potential variations in graphene layers. By applying the technique to a curved graphene layer, we investigated the local energy spectrum and confirmed the accuracy of our method by reproducing the predicted spectrum using an established formalism for a curved electron gas. Furthermore, our tool was utilized to study the local properties of a gated graphene layer on a substrate, demonstrating the significance of surface potential variations in understanding experimental outcomes. The findings of our study highlight the indispensable role of surface potential variations in characterizing local properties in graphene-based systems.

modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms: a quantum one for approximating Shannon entropy that requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries, and another for approximating von Neumann entropy that necessitates $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries. These results hold provided the entropy is bounded away from zero by a quantity linked to $\eta > 0$, and a no-go result indicates the non-existence of polynomial query algorithms for distributions with very low entropy. The analysis considers the most general input model - the quantum purified query access model - enabling handling of both classical distributions and quantum states. The study also establishes a lower bound on query complexity at $\Omega(n^{\frac{1}{3\gamma^2}})$ for approximating Shannon and von Neumann entropies in probability distributions and quantum states respectively.

Despite these high aspirations, current implementations of the concept fall short, often misinterpreting user input or requiring unnecessary technical expertise. Furthermore, by offloading cognitive burdens, computers can facilitate innovative interactions that would be impossible for humans to perform. The research provided empirical evidence to support these claims.

In a model designed to mimic cellular conditions, we have been studying the phase separation of a mix of proteins and nucleic acids within a chamber. Our system includes two types of proteins: one that naturally interacts with nucleic acids and immobilized proteins preventing them from moving. Protein-nucleic acid interactions are also hindered by high concentrations of a third component. The number and volume of droplets can be manipulated through varying the component's concentration, and our observations match the predictions from a simplified model, suggesting that droplet formation follows a universal growth law. Since many cellular phase separations share similarities with our model, our findings have the potential to shed light on the organization of cellular droplets and understand their underlying mechanics.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes can be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power-law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity requirement of the constraints, allowing a new property called d-extendable. The results also provide insight into fractional treewidth and explain certain classes that can be solved exactly in polynomial time.

However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic applications, based on the principles of recursive functions and the foundations of computation theory. By leveraging the work of Michael G. Kimkel and Christof Keller on recursive functions for RAMs, the underlying computation model is grounded in first-order logic, ensuring its correctness and adequacy. A novel RAM model features a finite, initially-filled memory with finite-wordlengths, accompanied by unlimited input and output capabilities. The existence of at least one base recursive function in the computation domain is also specified. The foundation provides a framework for the existence of specific computational tasks, such as sorting n elements, finding peaces of fixed size in graphs of size n, and solving the traveling salesman problem in n^(k+1) time, where k is the size of the input.

The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained by on-shell data, while off-shell data constrains the product of kinetic mixing and coupling of new vector boson with the Higgs boson. The constraints on kinetic coupling allow the coupling to be limited to approximately 0.7 times the equivalent coupling in the standard model.

Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory.

Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, enabling it to be used to guide the compact model's training. Notably, when access to the original data is not possible, we present a technique for estimating the resistance distances, which relies on generating adversarial examples to probe the network's decision boundaries. This results in reliable distillation results, even with limited resources. Overall, our approach offers a versatile and practical solution for training compact models in a variety of scenarios.

As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered that even though individual events may be random and discrete, they can often produce measurable and continuous outcomes. This concept has led to the development of methods for analytically quantifying complex phenomena, often observed in everyday life. In the context of road traffic, drivers might experience stopped waves – waves of drivers that slow down or stop due to traffic congestion – which, although produced by individual drivers' random decisions, can be modeled as a continuous phenomenon. Similarly, in this study, we explore the application of central limit theorem effects to simulate and study the outcomes of vehicle-vehicle collisions in road accidents. The use of statistical methods allows for the quantification of factors such as energy, damage, and number of vehicles involved in an accident, often documented in insurance databases and required for safety assessments. By applying the central limit theorem, we can gain a deeper understanding of the nature of car crashes and improve existing safety assessment methodologies.

formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby nearly doubling the cold gas within a 75 million-year period. Cloud expansion appears to be determined by factors such as density and localized heat-producing mechanisms that either cause the clouds to shrink and crumble or to grow through shattering. Magnetic fields are found to have a moderating effect on the cloud's growth while its topology plays a role in the evolution of both the cold and warm components. Conversely, anisotropic thermal conduction may cause the clouds to grow faster, thereby resulting in increased amounts of warm phase, contradicting commonly held assumptions. Ultimately, densely packed, magnetically bound structures are found to be long-lasting, thereby rendering them highly effective at producing massive star-forming regions.

This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved with the proposed units.

the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For very high mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear initially, but quickly weaken and then disappear completely, which makes it impossible for these low-velocity outflows to form early in the protostar formation process, especially in magnetic clouds that are very weak, leading to different star formation processes than what is typically observed.

to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. in next-generation in-flight entertainment systems, networking technology must be substantially enhanced. The current model is suited for data-centric systems but needs significant improvement for service availability in aircraft. The fundamental issue is the network's inability to respond to real-time changes, primarily due to its vulnerability to packet loss, delayed transmission, and unpredictable latency. To tackle these challenges, this research introduces a novel, fault-tolerant Many-to-Many transmission protocol called FMTM. Building on token passing, FMTM ensures reliable, error-correcting forward error correction to guarantee seamless operation in harsh wireless environments. Furthermore, a conservative scheduling algorithm combined with static scheduling provides predictable and efficient system functioning. The success of FMTM was verified through comprehensive simulations, which demonstrated the protocol's ability to correct transmission errors, maintain seamless service, and effectively manage network throughput to meet the complex requirements of high-throughput in-flight entertainment systems.

To tackle this issue, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing). We then outline general methods for validating the robustness of the models against all sorts of transformation-based attacks and showcase through practical examples the significant improvements that can be achieved using a much smaller number of validation points compared to the extensive point sets typically employed in literature. Additionally, we introduce and utilize "recomposition" as a unified validation method for various types of transformation-based attacks, thereby offering an adaptable and efficient solution that is largely independent of the specific type of transformation and can be easily generalized to other types of transformations. Our experiments reveal that employing recomposition yields notable improvements in performance and can be achieved with a reduced number of validation points compared to the traditional approach.

, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information technologies.

To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

aviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models.

Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's spontaneous breaking of a scale symmetry inherent to both dark matter and gravity.
The breaking of scale symmetry causes dark matter's momentum to be heavily linked with its mass, resulting in the conservation of total momentum-mass product (p-g-m).
Due to relativistic momentum's square being proportional to energy instead of the product of energy and a constant, the momentum-mass product's conservation leads to the momentum of massive objects disappearing at high velocities - an effect comparable to Einstein's theory of special relativity's (p/c)^2 = (E/c^2)m being a derivative model.
As a result, gravity's four-dimensional spacetime appears as a slightly modified outcome from the momentum-mass product's conservation in a vacuum state with no scale symmetry.
The almost imperceptible discrepancy between Einstein's and modern gravity's equations, when using the momentum-mass product's conservation, can explain the universe's accelerating expansion, thereby eliminating the need for dark energy.

of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic fields in a theoretical model developed in a previous study. It is now recognized that magnetic forces could play a more significant role than previously thought, especially in low-mass protostars. In cases where magnetic fields were relatively weak (less than 10^-4 strength compared to gravitational forces), protostars typically merged; however, if this value was above 10^-4, protostars generally remained separate. Once the protostars' magnetic properties reached a certain threshold (around 10^-6), flux-freezing often caused them to migrate to the disk's outer regions, potentially leading to gas and dust mass discrepancies. Ultimately, whether protostars merged or remained separate heavily influenced the initial mass function and, in cases of low-mass protostars, led to a shorter duration for gas and dust accumulation (by a factor of approximately ten).

The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for the complexities of modern machine learning systems, which often rely on an interdependent network of components, such as data augmenters, for their operation. The absence of methods to handle such systems has hindered the goal of accurately attributing errors or biases within these sophisticated models. This paper fills the gap by introducing a novel theoretical framework that allows for the computation of the Shapley value for a chain of dependent training examples within unified viewable Bayesian networks. The proposed framework successfully extends the scope of Shapley value computation from individual models to more advanced machine learning systems, thus providing a useful tool for the attribution of errors and biases within these systems.

cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. To evaluate the long-term stability of cryptocurrencies, we analyzed their annual growth rates and found that they remained within predictable limits, distinct from the unpredictable behavior of pure speculative assets. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. reaction $^{12}C + ^{12}C$ is investigated at a low energy range of 0.3-20 MeV with a focus on $\alpha$-particle separation energy of $^{20}$Ne. The present work updates and consolidates the existing data, including new findings from relevant experiments. A direct reaction method is employed to measure the fusion cross-section while evaporation residues are measured through a particle-activated technique. The experimental outcomes are as follows: The low-energy fusion cross-section matches well with theoretical calculations in the non-resonant energy range. A significant non-linear resonance is discovered at 19.37 MeV with a striking peak in the fusion cross-section, reaching 1.64 mb. This is notably higher than a previous finding and suggests a non-linear resonance at 20.40 MeV in the $^{12}C + ^{12}C$ energy scale. The $\alpha$-particle separation energy of $^{20}$Ne is determined to be $5.529 \pm 0.014$ MeV.

Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and training set choices. Consequently, uncertainty quantification has emerged as a critical companion to deep learning, with various methods such as Monte Carlo dropout, kernelized uncertainty, Variational Bayes, and Bayesian optimization actively being researched. This paper aims to synthesize the vast literature surrounding uncertainty quantification in deep learning, with a particular focus on spectral methods that efficiently harness the information content of data even with limited samples. Our objective is to delve into these techniques' theoretical underpinnings, examining the inherent trade-offs between predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation. Furthermore, we will explore recent applications in computer vision, geophysical flow simulation, quantum physics, medical imaging, and seismic imaging, highlighting the diverse potential of these methods to tackle a wide range of physics and engineering problems.

This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 5 GeV. This study is the first to demonstrate alterations in parton (dominated by quarks) showers traversing the QGP with a known initial trajectory, also offering a controlled comparison to test theoretical models.

Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor brown dwarf and possibly the initial instance of a Y subdwarf, necessitating further examination through broad-band spectroscopy and photometry using JWST for validation of the hypothesis that the object's abnormal color indices result from high-age, metal-poor atmosphere rather than deviating from traditional Y dwarf class.

This understanding has led to a theoretical model proposing two distinct regimes for a liquid film coating a fiber in an air-liquid environment. The "stick-slip" regime is characterized by liquid molecules adhering to the fiber, while the "slipper" regime features reduced friction between the fiber and the liquid. This theoretical model predicts the presence of two critical points, separating which distingu which regimes occur. The "stick-slip" regime is favored by low liquid viscosity and large fiber sizes, whereas the "slipper" regime prefers higher viscosity and smaller fiber sizes. The "slipper" regime is further distinguished by the presence of periodic droplet shedding from the fiber. The accuracy of this theoretical model was validated through experiments and direct numerical simulations. The findings from this study have implications for understanding how liquid films interact with slender objects and may lead to the development of novel methods for removing liquid from fibers and fibers in various applications where liquid film interactions are crucial.

Both pipelines rely on PAUS's near-infrared data and responsive spectral modeling to estimate star formation rates. However, these estimates are found to be consistently higher than actual values, especially for more distant galaxies. Ultimately, we identify a critical need for further work to improve these estimations, especially for more distant galaxies in our sight.

The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the plume gains mass, as well as the direction in which the particles move within the plume. The studies showed that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the movement of fluid into the plume increases significantly. The rate of fluid movement increased in direct proportion to the ratio of the particles' gain of mass to the fluid's gain of mass, and this increased rate was independent of particle size. In contrast, when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are the same, adding particles has no effect on fluid movement. The observed increase in fluid movement, which occurs when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, can be attributed to inertial clustering, a phenomenon where particles move to regions with high turbulence. The increased concentration of particles can cause convective instability in these areas, which grows and eventually significantly increases the rate at which fluid moves into the plume. The movements of fluid and particles that occur in rotating systems were similarly studied and showed distinct differences. The increased accumulation of particles in rotating systems causes convective instability that initially decreases the rate of fluid movement, which then increases as the system develops

Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the foundation for more comprehensive theories, such as superstrings.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials, thereby restricting the scope of viable models and requiring them to comply with these theoretical constraints to remain consistent with the principles of supergravity.  In an effort to overcome this limitation, a local approach to supergravity has been developed, allowing for more flexibility and thereby providing an opportunity to incorporate these cosmic applications into local supergravity theories, thereby addressing these limitations and opening up the space of viable models.  In this context, an overview of local supergravity, an extension of the supergravity framework in which the spin-3/2 gravitational field possesses both left- and right-handed components, will be provided, along with a discussion of the incorporation of isoscalar deformations, thereby allowing for an examination of the cosmic applications of this theoretical framework, such as cosmological inflation, within a local supergravity context.

This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.

The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.

First, we utilize a novel, flexible framework to develop efficient pruning techniques that maintain high accuracy with minimal neurons. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by substituting untested actions with their worst-case values, ensuring a guaranteed lower limit on the true optimal value. Our approach extends this strategy to creating a Bayesian Q-function network that, when plugged into a Bayesian machine learning method, maintains pessimism's guarantee. Our method, which includes a variety of network structures such as linear, decision tree, and neural networks, is thoroughly examined in simulation studies across various contexts. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. In such cases, researchers often employ mathematical operations like adding weights to the data or converting it into different matrices to capture distinct aspects of their subject matter of interest. These modifications can sometimes be interpreted as combining presence-absence data with numerical information. However, we argue that multiple-valued data presents different challenges and considerations, requiring a different theoretical foundation than the traditional handling of presence-absence data. Through examples and a matrix association theorem, we demonstrate the need for a new theoretical framework that addresses the unique aspects of multiple-valued data, even when its interpretation solely stems from the data itself and not additional metrics.

deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics.

2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse radon transform followed by a deconvolution process to compensate for partial x-ray attenuation. However, conventional methods often utilize single energy-source projections, which necessitate costly iterative corrections to produce high-quality images. In an effort to simplify the image-reconstruction process, a new study employs simultaneous low-dose X-ray scans from both sides of a CT scanner, utilizing a translational resolution of 1mm that surpasses conventional lateral resolution of 5mm. As a result, image quality is significantly enhanced and objects as far apart as 65mm in diameter can be distinctively separated. In the context of conventional CT scanners, which produce images of the heart, liver, and lungs, this improved resolution would yield more accurate cardiac risk assessments, enhance liver tumor detection, and boost lung cancer diagnosis accuracy. Furthermore, the increased resolution would enable safer low-dose CT scans in children, which could greatly contribute to their health and well-being. In the field of engineering, objects such as small-sized hollow cylinders and details on fractured bones would be more accurately examined.

A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. With this modified understanding of the bulk-point limit, the model can accurately reproduce scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space.

Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr framework, which automatically detects SMMO applications, distributes them to GPUs, and applies parallel processing through dynamic memory allocation and parallel method execution.  Our experimental results demonstrate that DynaSOAr successfully accelerates a range of real-world applications, achieving significant speedups on a range of systems, including single-GPU and multi-GPU configurations.

To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a Dirac fermion χ as a dark matter candidate that's odd under gauged Z2 symmetry post U(1)X breaking, leading to a natural realization of isospin-violating dark matter with a natural f_n/f_p ratio of -0.7, thereby evading LUX, PANDAX and XENON1T experimental constraints. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible probability that a decision function fails given the unknown parameters' possible range – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit with constrained probabilities. Utilizing an efficient reduction method from deterministic circuits, we present a polynomial-time solution to MARmax that does not require computational complexity to scale, even with deterministic circuits of arbitrary size. Additionally, our proposed method demonstrates significant computational efficiency in diverse benchmark case studies, which also explore the impact of parameter uncertainty on MARmax.

the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, utilizing the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$, a detailed study was conducted on the CMZ to determine how gas density varies in different directions. The results show that the anisotropy parameter $A$ ranges from approximately 0.75 to 0.05 as the gas density increases, which can be explained by three distinct modes: diffuse, organized, and chaotic. The CMZ is currently undergoing the fragmentation of its gas due to star formation, which is influencing the distribution of its components and shaping their structures. The discovery of its anisotropy also places the CMZ in the same category as star-forming regions like R136 and the Quintuplet Cluster, which are renowned for their isotropic properties. Moreover, by simulating the formation of clumps in a randomly agitated gas cloud, the researchers found a positive correlation between anisotropy and fragmentation, which supports the hypothesis that the CMZ's clumps may soon reach their critical mass and turn into stars.

in quantum information science and has far-reaching implications in both theoretical and practical research. As a multifaceted phenomenon, entanglement has been pivotal in generating quantum teleportation, quantum cryptography, quantum key distribution, and quantum computing. Despite its significance, accurately measuring entanglement remains a complex task. Therefore, developing versatile and reliable methods for entanglement measurement is a pressing research requirement to tackle these challenges. In response to these ongoing difficulties, this study makes groundbreaking contributions by proposing a two-sphere method for entanglement measurement. Unlike conventional approaches that struggle with partial transposes, this method seamlessly handles entanglement measurement for arbitrary pure states on Hilbert spaces of dimensions (d1+d2), even when d1 and d2 differ. Its broad applicability enables entanglement measurement for a wide range of quantum systems, as well as deriving concurrence formulas for various entanglement measures, including von Neumann, Lin, and concurrence with respect to the arbitrary product states (CP). In addition, CP enables a thorough examination of entanglement properties, leading to its application in diverse quantum systems, including Hilbert spaces of dimensions 4 and 6. Furthermore, CP is linked to the two-sphere geometric approach, extending its scope to arbitrary pure states on these spheres. In contrast to existing methods, the two-sphere method exhibits exceptional versatility in its applications.

Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below $0.5$, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded $0.5$, two distinct non-standard polar crystalline phases emerged alongside the non-polar hexagonal crystal structure, namely the antiferroelectric splay crystal and the ferroelectric splay crystal. In order to study all of these configurations, we evaluated their characteristics in terms of the pair correlation function, radial distribution function of molecules, and nematic and ferroelectric order parameters.

The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this by leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometry, coupled with the use of a single-pixel imaging method. By doing so, we have successfully performed interaction-free imaging of a structured object using undetected photons, thus pushing the boundaries of quantum imaging to the point where object interaction and photon detection are minimized. This innovation lays the groundwork for utilizing single-pixel imaging to examine delicate samples while minimizing harm from light interaction and eliminating the need for detection.

A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization the next time around. In this research, a class of quartic graphs known as accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which will be denoted as A[n,k]. It has been shown that each member of A[n,k] has the PH-property, expanding the family initially identified by Alahmadi et al. Furthermore, a combinatorial argument can be employed to demonstrate that a specified condition - 2k being a perfect matching number of G - is necessary for a graph G to belong to A[n,k]. Utilizing this necessary condition, it becomes feasible to develop a centralized algorithm that generates all possible members of A[n,k] for a given k. In addition, it has been found that the PH-property is not confined to accordion graphs, which prompts the investigation of the essential differences between these two graph families.

By utilizing the Yosida approximate identity at the boundary of the spectrum, we show that a scaled evolution operator converges to a self-adjoint limit symbol, which governs the asymptotic behavior. The symbol's spectrum determines the outcome: the quantum walk remains trapped in the subspace if the spectrum remains isolated, while it escapes to the full Hilbert space if the spectrum intersects. We verify this method by studying two specific limiting cases, and then devise a way to control escape times by designing a family of trapping states with adjustable lifetimes.

Our research shows that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a capability absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our study highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, utilizing large image patches (16x16), and selecting diversity data samples to maximize the quality of the learned semantic structure. Building upon this foundation, we developed FlowPerm, a novel permutation inference method, which demonstrates that there indeed exists a semantic structure underlying an image space that can be learned through self-supervised ViT. When applied to ImageNet, FlowPerm reveals a hierarchical taxonomy consistent with the actual ImageNet hierarchy, showcasing the potential of permuting unordered image data to expose latent semantics.

models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), a novel strategy involving the deliberate manipulation of semantic vectors to regulate the image generation process. By doing so, the artist achieves a level of influence comparable to the image's original text input, enabling them to produce a coherent, high-quality image or image series from a base diffusion model.

a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude.

These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of area, diameter, and speed. The results indicate that these characteristics exhibit two-component structures, pointing to the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points, associated with different types of magnetic flux elements, and influenced by the underlying magnetic field topology. This study's findings can be interpreted in the context of the magnetic field's varying complexity and dynamics, observed on the solar surface.
